newsitem.title: FRANCE: Catholic hero or war criminal?.
newsitem.headline: Catholic hero or war criminal?.

text.p: Pope John Paul steps into a historical controversy on Sunday when he honours a fifth century king seen by some as the founder of Christian France but by others as a Dark Ages war criminal.

The Pontiff will upset many merely by attending celebrations in the city of Reims of the 1,500th anniversary of the baptism of Clovis, a pagan king who was the first west European monarch to convert to Roman Catholicism.
To traditionalists, Clovis' conversion was France's baptism as a nation, making it the "eldest daughter of the Church".
French monarchs before the 1789 Revolution regarded him as their spiritual forefather -- the 16 kings called Louis were using a modern version of Clovis' name.
Yet to some historians, Clovis was a brutal Frankish warlord devoid of religious convictions who converted merely to enlist Church backing against rival tribes like the Visigoths.

"If Clovis is undeniably part of the history of our country, it's in the same way Radovan Karadzic will feature in the history of Serbia," wrote journalist Dominique Jamet in one of several iconoclastic books about Clovis.
Karadzic, leader of the Bosnian Serbs, was forced from office in July by international pressure after he was indicted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague.

The Clovis anniversary has become the focus of twin controversies over his suitability for commemoration and over whether President Jacques Chirac is violating the separation of church and state by helping sponsor the papal trip.

The Pontiff implied on his first visit in 1980 that France was rightfully Catholic in what critics saw both as a swipe at official secularism, and as a negation of the country's other religious communities -- Moslems, Protestants and Jews.

"France, eldest daughter of the church, what have you done with the promises of your baptism?", he asked at Le Bourget near Paris, referring to Clovis' conversion around the year 496. Other dates cited by historians are 498, 499 or 506.

Bernard Lagoutte, secretary general of the French Bishops' Conference, said the Pope was not coming "to call for a Catholic France or to give lessons about morality...He's coming to remind Catholics of the importance of their own baptism."
He said the Pope would be careful to avoid suggesting that Clovis's baptism made France a Catholic country.

Clovis, who lived from 466-511 and inspired myths about a divine link between French monarchs and God, has been hijacked as a symbol by the anti-immigrant National Front, which says white, Christian French civilisation is superior to others.
"Let us together celebrate the 1,500th anniversary of the French nation, so it may one day again live in its former splendour," say pro-National Front "Clovis Committee" leaflets.

A militant secularist group responded with posters of a black Ivory Coast-born student who rejoices in the name of Clovis Achi. "My name's Clovis. I'm 18 years old. French history is mine too," the caption says.
Achi told Reuters his name was not a political statement. "My family obviously liked monarchs. One of my cousins is named Baudouin" after the late Belgian king, he said.

Anti-papal activists, who plan a protest rally in Paris as the Pontiff prays in Reims, accuse the government of pandering to the far right and to traditionalist Catholics by whooping up the obscure anniversary.

France has minted Clovis coins and the post office is to issue Clovis stamps. The city of Reims has used public funds to sponsor exhibitions controversially entitled "Clovis, or the baptism of France".

Michel Rouche, a historian at Paris' Sorbonne university and author of "Clovis", said Chirac was being criticised unfairly. It was the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand who laid guidelines for the papal trip in 1993, he said.

What little is known about Clovis, a shadowy pagan general allied with Rome whose heraldic symbol was a toad, comes from the writings of priest Gregoire de Tours, who chronicled his reign more than half a century after the king died.
Born in Kortrijk, now in Belgium, Clovis ruled a kingdom spanning western parts of the Netherlands and Germany, Belgium, Luxembourg and eastern France at the time of his baptism.
He went on to conquer most of western and southwestern France, making Paris his capital.
Clovis promised his Catholic wife Clothilde he would convert if her God helped him win the battle of Tolbiac against the Visigoths in 496. He duly won and was baptised in Reims.
Pierre Berge, author of "The Clovis Affair", said the battlefield of Tolbiac, near modern-day Cologne in Germany, would have been a better site for any commemoration of Clovis.
It would deflate French chauvinism and appease European Union partners by showing that much of Clovis' kingdom was outside France, he said.

Clovis was never made a saint, although Catholic lore says a white dove came from heaven at his baptism. He continued to slaughter his relatives to eliminate potential rivals even after his conversion.

Pre-revolutionary Church and royal apologists explained away the massacres as a way of uniting a nascent France. Modern historians say they were common in an age when kings saw no contradiction in being a Catholic hero and a war criminal.
